title: The Body in Grief
hook: Grief folds the body inward around what it has lost, and the most useful thing another body can do is stay near it.
why:
Everyone grieves, and almost everyone is unsure what to do when someone else is grieving. Men in particular are often given few words and fewer models: stand at the graveside, shake hands, say *sorry for your loss*, and then go back to normal. Meanwhile the grieving man's body tells a long story that most people around him do not know how to read, and some read badly, deciding that he is not grieving enough, or too much, or in the wrong way.

This chapter is about reading grief and staying with it. You will learn what grief does to the body, why grieving people move back and forth between sorrow and ordinary life, how grief can strain the heart in the most literal sense, why people grieve in different styles, what helps and what does not, how grief comes in waves long after others have moved on, and when grief that has become stuck needs more than friends can give. The chapter on the quiet body in Part VI said the end of all this skill is a presence other people can rest in. Nowhere does that matter more than here.

teach.p:
Grief is not only a feeling. It is a full-body state, and much of it is visible. Crying, of course, and the breath patterns of crying described in the chapter on breath, but also frequent sighing, a heavy tiredness, slowed movement and a body that seems to curl around itself: shoulders rounded, head bowed, arms wrapped around the chest or the knees, the face in the hands. The grief plates in the pose library show some of these shapes.

Grief also disrupts the body's routines. Sleep breaks up. Appetite disappears or turns to comfort eating. Concentration fails, and grieving people often describe a fog: losing keys, forgetting appointments, reading the same paragraph again and again. Some feel physical pain, a heaviness in the chest, a tightness in the throat. Some become restless, unable to sit, walking for hours. Some look for the person who has died, turning at a familiar voice in a crowd, expecting them to come through the door.

None of this is a sign that something is wrong with the grieving person. It is what bodies do after a loss, and it can last much longer than people around the bereaved expect: months, and in waves for years.

For a reader, the lesson is to expect grief to show, and to show differently in different people. Some will be visibly undone. Some will look almost unchanged in public and collapse in private. The grief plates are not a checklist. They are a reminder that the body carries loss, and that what you see is only part of what is there.

Do not measure someone's grief by how much of it you can see.
teach.disconfirm: If bereaved people showed no more disruption of sleep, appetite, concentration and movement than anyone else, grief would be a feeling without a body. The experience of almost everyone who has grieved, and the research described below, suggest otherwise.
teach.pullQuote: Do not measure someone's grief by how much of it you can see.

teach.p:
People often imagine grief as a steady state that slowly fades, or as a series of stages to be passed through in order. In 1999 Margaret Stroebe and Henk Schut proposed a different picture, which they called the dual process model. Grieving people, they argued, move back and forth between two kinds of activity. In loss-oriented moments they face the loss directly: crying, remembering, looking at photographs, yearning. In restoration-oriented moments they turn to the business of living: sorting out the house, going back to work, learning new tasks, taking a break from grief by watching a film or seeing friends. Both are part of healthy grieving, and the movement between them is the point.

This explains something that often confuses observers. A widower laughing at the wake, a son joking with his brothers the day after their father's death, a mother going back to work a week after a funeral: none of them is failing to grieve. They are in a restoration moment, and the loss will come back.

Research by George Bonanno and colleagues has added a further surprise: many bereaved people show considerable resilience, functioning reasonably well within months, without this meaning they loved the person less. In one study of bereaved spouses, Dacher Keltner and Bonanno found that genuine laughter while talking about the person who had died went with less distress, not more, and with warmer responses from others.

So read grief over time, not in a single moment. A grieving man who is smiling today may be in pieces tomorrow, and both are real.
teach.disconfirm: If grieving people who laughed, worked and took breaks from sorrow early on later fared worse than those who grieved continuously, the dual process view would be wrong. The research described here found the opposite, though every person's path is different.

teach.p:
The phrase *a broken heart* is more than a metaphor. In 2012 Elizabeth Mostofsky and colleagues studied nearly two thousand people who had had a heart attack and compared the timing of the attack with recent losses in their lives. In the twenty-four hours after the death of someone significant to them, the rate of heart attacks was about twenty-one times higher than usual. The risk fell steadily over the following days and weeks.

The numbers behind that estimate are small, and the absolute risk for any one bereaved person remains low. But the finding fits what is known about grief as a stress state: a racing heart, raised blood pressure, broken sleep, missed meals and forgotten medication, all at once, in people who may already have heart disease. Doctors also recognise a rarer condition, sometimes called broken heart syndrome, in which sudden severe emotional stress temporarily weakens the heart muscle.

For a reader, this has practical consequences. In the days after a death, look out for the bereaved, especially older people and those with heart conditions. Make sure they are eating, sleeping where possible and taking their usual medication. Do not dismiss chest pain, breathlessness or fainting as grief; call for medical help.

It also makes sense of something many bereaved people describe: a physical ache in the chest. It is real, and it is worth taking seriously.

In the first days after a loss, care for the body as well as the heart.
teach.disconfirm: If heart attacks were no more common in the days after a significant death than at other times, the physical warning in this block would be unnecessary. The study found a sharp rise, though based on a small number of cases, so it is a reason for care rather than alarm.

teach.p:
Kenneth Doka and Terry Martin, in *Grieving Beyond Gender*, describe a continuum of grieving styles. At one end is intuitive grieving, in which grief is felt and expressed mainly through emotion: crying, talking about feelings, seeking comfort from others. At the other is instrumental grieving, in which grief is experienced more through thought and expressed mainly through activity: doing things, solving problems, building, organising, remembering the person by acting for them. Most people blend the two.

Doka and Martin originally linked these styles to gender, and many men do lean towards the instrumental end, but they later stressed that gender is only one influence among many, and that plenty of women grieve instrumentally and plenty of men intuitively.

Instrumental grief is often misread. A man who rarely cries, goes back to work quickly, throws himself into sorting out the estate or rebuilding the garden, or organises a charity run in his late wife's name, may be judged by others as cold or as avoiding his grief. He may be grieving deeply, in the way that is most natural to him. Pressing him to talk about his feelings may feel like being asked to grieve in a foreign language.

The practical lesson is to meet people in their style. For an intuitive griever, sitting and talking may be the help. For an instrumental griever, working alongside him, side by side, on a task connected to the person who died, may let him talk in a way that a conversation across a table never would.

Grief that looks like doing is still grief.
teach.disconfirm: If people who grieved mainly through activity fared consistently worse than those who grieved mainly through talking and tears, instrumental grief would be avoidance rather than a style. Doka and Martin's work suggests the styles are different paths, not better and worse ones.

teach.h: What helps, and what does not.
teach.p:
The most useful thing you can offer a grieving person is presence. Turn up. Sit with them. Say the name of the person who died, because many bereaved people say that what hurts most is everyone else avoiding it. Ask about them: *Tell me about him.* Let silences happen.

Practical help often matters more than words. Meals, lifts, help with forms and phone calls, mowing the lawn, picking up children, sorting the post. Offer specific things rather than *let me know if you need anything*, which puts the burden of asking on the person least able to bear it. *I'm bringing dinner on Thursday. Is six all right?* is easier to accept.

Some well-meant phrases tend to hurt. *At least he had a long life*, *everything happens for a reason*, *she's in a better place*, *I know how you feel*, *you need to be strong for the children*: each tries to shrink or explain the loss, and many bereaved people describe them as the hardest things they heard. A simple *I'm so sorry* and your continued presence say more.

Touch may help, or it may not. The chapter on touch said to ask, and grief does not change that. An open hand, an arm offered, sitting close enough that they can lean on you if they want to, leave the choice with them.

And do not disappear. Most support arrives in the first fortnight and fades after the funeral. The months after, when the casseroles stop and everyone else has moved on, are often the hardest. Put the anniversary in your calendar.
teach.disconfirm: If bereaved people reported that platitudes such as at least he had a long life helped as much as presence, practical help and hearing the name of the person who died, this block's advice would not matter. Bereaved people's accounts consistently suggest otherwise.

teach.p:
Long after the funeral, grief keeps coming back, often suddenly. A song in a shop, a smell, a date, a place, a photograph found in a drawer, the first Christmas, the birthday, the anniversary: any of these can bring a wave of grief as strong as the first days, months or even years later. Bereaved people often describe being ambushed by it.

The body shows the wave. A man in a supermarket may suddenly go still, his breath catching, and walk out leaving his trolley. A colleague may leave a meeting abruptly and come back ten minutes later with red eyes. A friend at a wedding may go quiet during the father-and-daughter dance. To an observer who does not know the history, these moments can look like rudeness, illness or moodiness.

For a reader, two things follow. First, keep a longer memory of other people's losses than they might expect you to. Note the anniversary of a friend's bereavement. Be gentle around birthdays, holidays and the dates you know about. A message on the first anniversary, *thinking of you and of her today*, often means more than anything said at the funeral.

Second, when someone suddenly withdraws, goes quiet or leaves, put grief on your list of rivals, especially if you know of a loss. Do not demand an explanation. A quiet *you all right?* later, or simply making space, is enough.

A wave is not a relapse. It is grief doing what grief does.
teach.disconfirm: If grief, once it had eased, did not return in waves around anniversaries and reminders, the advice to remember dates would matter less. Most bereaved people describe exactly these waves, often years later.

teach.p:
For most people, grief changes over time. It does not disappear, but it becomes something they can carry alongside their lives. For a minority, it does not: months later, the yearning is as intense as at the start, the person cannot accept the death, life has lost all meaning, and they cannot function at work or at home. Psychiatry now recognises this as prolonged grief disorder. The World Health Organization's classification looks for it at least six months after a death, and the American system at least twelve months.

You are not in a position to diagnose it, and should not try. What you can notice is a pattern that has not shifted at all after many months: a person who has stopped functioning, stopped eating properly, cut themselves off from everyone, is drinking heavily, or speaks of wanting to be with the person who died.

When you see that pattern, encourage the person to talk to their doctor. Specialist bereavement support and therapies for prolonged grief exist and help. Many areas have bereavement services that people can contact directly. Offer practical help in getting there.

And if a grieving person says they want to join the person who died, or that they cannot go on without them, take it seriously. Ask them directly whether they are thinking of ending their life. Grief is a time of raised risk, and asking does not put the idea in their head. The chapter on suicidal ideation explains how to respond, and the crisis resources are one tap from the home screen.

Most grief needs company. Some grief needs more, and part of staying near is noticing when.
teach.disconfirm: If grief that remained intense and disabling many months after a loss eased just as well without specialist help as with it, encouraging professional support would add little. The recognition of prolonged grief disorder reflects evidence that some people need, and benefit from, more.

poseGallery.doCaption: 'I'm so sorry. Tell me about him.'
poseGallery.dontCaption: 'At least he had a long life.'
poseGallery.annotation: Platitudes try to shrink the loss. Presence, and hearing the name of the person who died, help far more.

poseGallery.doCaption: Knowing grief comes and goes, and some people grieve by doing.
poseGallery.dontCaption: Deciding he can't have cared, since he's back at work and joking.
poseGallery.annotation: Grieving people move between sorrow and ordinary life, and instrumental grievers express grief through action. Neither means less love.

poseGallery.doCaption: Turning up in month three with a meal, and on the anniversary.
poseGallery.dontCaption: Disappearing once the funeral is over.
poseGallery.annotation: Support fades after the first fortnight, when the hardest months begin. Remembering later often means the most.

poseGallery.doCaption: Sitting close, and leaving the choice of touch to him.
poseGallery.dontCaption: Hugging him because he looks like he needs it.
poseGallery.annotation: Grief does not change the rule on touch. Offer, sit close enough to lean on, and let the grieving person choose.

poseGallery.doCaption: A neighbour at his table in month three
poseGallery.dontCaption: A widower left alone once the funeral is over
poseGallery.annotation: Visitors fall away after the funeral, just as the hardest months begin. A cup of tea and her name said aloud are remembered for years.

poseGallery.doCaption: A walk together, and his name said aloud
poseGallery.annotation: Avoiding the name of the person who died can be the loneliest part of grief. Say it, and let the stories come.

caseStudy:
Andy, forty, and his sister Claire lose their mother in February. Their father, Bill, sixty-seven, has been married to her for forty-four years. At the funeral he shakes every hand and does not cry. A week later he is back at his allotment, and then he starts rebuilding the shed she always complained about. Claire tells Andy, upset, that Dad does not seem to care.

Andy is not so sure. He has noticed that Bill's walk has slowed, that he sighs often, that he has stopped eating breakfast, and that he works on the shed from first light until dark. He has also noticed that Bill always takes his heart pills with breakfast, and wonders whether he is taking them now. He asks. Bill admits he has forgotten them most days. Andy puts them by the kettle with a note.

Andy does not ask his father how he is feeling. He turns up on Saturdays with his tools, and they work on the shed together, side by side. On the third Saturday, measuring a window frame, Bill says that Mum wanted a window just here so she could watch the birds, and that he is building it the way she wanted. Then he talks about her for an hour while they work, more than he has talked about anything in years.

Andy explains to Claire what he has seen: that Dad is grieving by building, and that it is real. Claire starts bringing lunch on Saturdays.

On the anniversary in February, Andy rings in the morning. Bill's voice catches on the first word, and he says he is fine, and then that he is not, and then that he is glad Andy rang. In the spring they put a bird feeder outside the new window.
observe: Think of someone you know who has been bereaved in the past year, and notice whether they seem to grieve more by feeling or by doing.
Notice the phrases people use to comfort the bereaved, and which ones try to shrink or explain the loss.
Look through your calendar and note any anniversaries of losses among people close to you.

drills.name: Name and Calendar
steps: List the people close to you who have lost someone in the past two years.
For each, note the name of the person who died, if you know it.
Find out, if you can, the date of the death or the funeral.
Put a reminder in your calendar a day before each anniversary.
On the day, send a short message that mentions the person by name.
variations: Add the birthdays of the people who died, as well as the anniversaries of their deaths.
Send one message this month to someone whose loss was more than a year ago, mentioning the person by name.

drills.name: Specific Offers
steps: Write down three things you have said, or heard said, to bereaved people that put the burden of asking on them, such as let me know if you need anything.
For each, write a specific offer instead, with a day and time.
Write three phrases you will avoid and what you will say instead.
Say the specific offers aloud.
Use one of them the next time someone you know is bereaved.
variations: Write specific offers suited to different people: a parent, a colleague, a neighbour, a friend far away.
Ask someone who has been bereaved which offers they most valued and which they never took up.

drills.name: Style Check
steps: Think back to a loss in your own life.
Write down what you did in the weeks after it: what you felt, what you said, what you did with your hands and your time.
Mark whether your grief leaned towards feeling or towards doing.
Note how other people responded to your way of grieving.
Write what would have helped most, given your style.
variations: Think about how someone close to you grieved, and whether their style was different from yours.
Write what you would want people to do for you if you were bereaved, given your style, and share it with someone close.

drills.name: Side-by-Side Support
steps: Think of someone grieving who seems to grieve by doing rather than talking.
Identify a task connected to their loss, or simply a practical task they need done.
Offer to help with it, alongside them.
While you work, follow their lead in conversation; do not steer it towards feelings.
Afterwards, note anything they said about the person who died.
variations: Offer to help with a task linked to the person who died, such as sorting photographs or tending a grave, if the bereaved person wants it.
Note how the conversation changes when you are working alongside someone compared with sitting opposite them.

drills.name: Know the Thresholds
steps: Write down the signs in this chapter that grief may have become stuck.
Write down the signs that a grieving person may be at risk, including talk of wanting to join the person who died.
Find bereavement support services available where you live and note how to contact them.
Find the crisis resources in this app for your region.
Keep these notes where you can find them.
variations: Find out whether there is a bereavement service for children where you live, in case you ever need it for a family you know.
Write down how you would tell a child about a death in plain, honest words, avoiding phrases such as "gone to sleep".

quiz.q: Three weeks after his wife's funeral, a colleague is back at work, busy and even joking. What does this chapter suggest?
options: That he cannot have been very close to her, given how quickly he has recovered
That he is in denial and should be encouraged to talk about his feelings
That grief comes and goes, and some people grieve by doing; keep checking in
That he is fully over the loss and no longer needs any support at all
quiz.explain: Grieving people move between facing the loss and attending to life, and instrumental grievers express grief through action. Neither means less love. Keep remembering, especially in the months ahead and on the anniversary.

quiz.q: What does Stroebe and Schut's dual process model of grief propose?
options: Bereaved people move back and forth between facing the loss and attending to life
Bereaved people pass through five fixed stages of grief in a set order
Bereaved people who take breaks from grieving are avoiding their loss
Bereaved people should face the loss continuously until the grief has gone
quiz.explain: Both loss-oriented moments, such as crying and remembering, and restoration-oriented ones, such as work and distraction, are part of healthy grieving. The movement between them is the point.

quiz.q: What did Mostofsky and colleagues find in the twenty-four hours after the death of someone significant?
options: Heart attacks became less common, as people rested more after a death
There was no change at all in the rate of heart attacks after a death
Heart attacks became more common only among people under forty years old
The rate of heart attacks was about twenty-one times higher than usual
quiz.explain: The rate was sharply raised in the first day and fell steadily afterwards. The numbers were small and the absolute risk remains low, but it is a reason to look after the bereaved physically, especially those with heart conditions.

quiz.q: A friend's father has just died. What is most likely to help in the first weeks?
options: Telling him that at least his father lived a long and full life
Turning up, offering specific help, and saying his father's name
Waiting until he gets in touch, so that you do not intrude on him
Reminding him that he needs to be strong for the rest of the family
quiz.explain: Presence, practical help offered with a day and time, and hearing the name of the person who died help most. Platitudes and waiting to be asked tend to leave grieving people more alone.

quiz.q: What do Doka and Martin call grief that is experienced and expressed mainly through thought and activity rather than open emotion?
options: Delayed grief
Absent grief
Instrumental grieving
Complicated or prolonged grief
quiz.explain: Instrumental grievers often express grief by doing, building or organising, and are often misread as not grieving. It is a style, not a failure, and meeting them side by side, in action, often helps them talk.

quiz.q: Eight months after her husband died, your aunt barely leaves the house, has stopped eating properly, and says she just wants to be with him. What fits this chapter?
options: Ask her directly if she is thinking of ending her life, and help her reach help
Reassure her that time heals everything and that she will feel better soon
Leave her be, since grief is private and must simply be waited out
Tell her she is grieving the wrong way and needs to move on with her life
quiz.explain: Wanting to be with the person who died is a reason to ask directly about suicide, which does not plant the idea. Combined with months of withdrawal and not eating, it also suggests she needs more than company, so help her reach her doctor or a crisis line.

quiz.q: What pattern did George Bonanno's research find in many bereaved people?
options: Resilience: real sorrow, with little lasting disruption to daily life
Collapse: almost everyone stopped functioning for at least two whole years
Indifference: most people felt very little and returned to normal within days
Stages: nearly everyone moved through five fixed stages in exactly the same order
quiz.explain: Bonanno found that many bereaved people show resilience, real sorrow with little lasting disruption, and that this did not mean they loved the person less. Not crying is not a problem in itself.

quiz.q: Six weeks after his wife's funeral, your elderly neighbour's curtains stay shut at midday, his milk is left out and his car has not moved. What fits this chapter best?
options: Leave him alone, since grieving people always want privacy in the first months
Ring the police at once, since something terrible has certainly happened to him
Knock with a practical offer, say his wife's name and offer something specific
Push a leaflet about bereavement counselling through his door and leave it there
quiz.explain: A practical reason to knock is easy to accept, saying her name makes it safe to grieve, and a specific offer is more useful than "let me know if you need anything". Keep an eye on the signs that he needs more help.

quiz.q: Someone says that grief moves through five fixed stages, in order, and that a person who skips one is not grieving properly. What does this chapter say?
options: It is right, since research shows that every bereaved person follows these stages
Research does not find most people follow fixed stages; grief comes and goes
It is right for adults, though children move through the stages twice as quickly
It is right, but only for people who have lost a husband or a wife
quiz.explain: The stages come from Kübler-Ross's work with dying patients and were not meant as a fixed sequence. Research on bereavement finds people moving back and forth between grief and ordinary life, in no set order.

reflection.prompt: Think of one specific loss in your own life, or in the life of someone close to you. Describe what grief did to the body: sleep, appetite, movement, breath, concentration. Did the grief lean more towards feeling or towards doing? What did other people say or do that helped, and what hurt? Then think of someone you know who is grieving now or will be soon. What specific thing could you do in the months after the funeral, when most support fades?
reflection.guidance: Many men find that their own grief was misread, or that they misread someone else's, because it looked like doing rather than feeling. Try to describe the body before the emotion. The last question should produce something concrete, with a date if possible: a meal, a visit, a message on an anniversary.

failureMode: The commonest failure is to judge grief by how it looks, deciding that someone who is working, joking or dry-eyed cannot really be grieving, or that someone still weeping months later is grieving wrong. The second is to reach for platitudes that shrink the loss. The third is to offer vague help, *let me know if you need anything*, and then to disappear after the funeral, just as the hardest months begin. The fourth is to miss the body: the forgotten medication, the chest pain dismissed as grief, the meals not eaten. And the most serious is to hear a grieving person say they want to join the one they lost and to let it pass. Stay near, offer specific help, remember the dates, and when grief is stuck or someone is at risk, help them reach more.

moreCases.title: The widow who laughed at the wake
moreCases.scene:
Pauline, seventy, buried her husband, Frank, on a Thursday morning after fifty-one years of marriage. At the wake, in the function room of the pub where they had their wedding reception, she moves from table to table. She tells stories about Frank: the time he drove to Blackpool with the handbrake on, the time he tried to teach the grandchildren to fish and fell in. People laugh, and so does she, loudly. She has a gin and tonic in her hand and is smiling.

Her daughter-in-law, Kerry, watching from the corner, says quietly to her husband that his mother does not seem very upset. "She's laughing like it's a party," she says. "I thought she'd be in pieces."

An hour later, Kerry goes to the ladies' and finds Pauline alone in there, sitting on the closed lid of a toilet with the cubicle door open, bent double, sobbing, Frank's reading glasses in her hand.

Pauline had chosen the pub herself. She said Frank would have hated a church hall and loved the jukebox, and she had put his favourite song on it before the first guests arrived.

Pauline's sister, who arrived from Spain that morning, stays close to her all afternoon, refilling her glass and laughing at every story, even the ones she has heard a hundred times. Twice she touches Pauline's elbow and steers her towards a chair, and twice Pauline shakes her head and keeps going.
moreCases.misread:
Kerry read Pauline's laughter and stories as a sign that she was not grieving much, because she expected grief to look like sadness all the time. She judged the grief by its appearance at one moment, in one setting.

She also judged it from the outside of a family she had joined only ten years before, without the fifty years of stories that made the laughter make sense.

She also missed what was happening around Pauline: the sister's steering hand, the refilled glass, the stories that never quite stopped. A widow who keeps moving at her husband's wake is often a widow who cannot yet bear to stand still.
moreCases.betterRead:
Stroebe and Schut's dual process model describes grieving people moving back and forth between facing the loss and turning to the business of living. At a wake, many people do both within minutes: telling stories, laughing, greeting people, then being ambushed by the full weight of the loss. Laughter about the person who died is often a way of being close to them, and many families describe the stories at the wake as among the most precious moments of the day. Neither the laughter nor the sobbing was the "real" grief. Both were. Kerry's better response, once she understood, was to sit beside Pauline in the cubicle, say nothing for a while, and then say, "He was so funny, wasn't he?" Pauline laughed through her tears and told her about the handbrake again.

Kerry said afterwards that she had learned more about grief in that cubicle than in her whole life before.

Pauline told her, later, that the laughing had been for Frank and the crying had been for herself, and that she needed both.

moreCases.title: The young man who went to the gym
moreCases.scene:
Kieran, twenty-two, lost his closest friend, Josh, in a road accident in the spring. At the funeral he stood at the back with his hands in his pockets and left before the wake. Since then he has been at the gym twice a day, has taken on extra shifts at work, and has stopped going out with the group of friends he and Josh shared. He does not mention Josh at all.

His mother, Sinéad, is worried. She has read that men bottle things up, and she keeps asking him to talk to her about how he feels. Each time, Kieran says he is fine and leaves the room. She has left leaflets about counselling on his bed. He has thrown them away.

His uncle, Declan, who lost his own brother young, suggests to Sinéad that she might be asking the wrong question.

Kieran has also started running at night, alone, sometimes for two hours. His mother hears him come in at one in the morning and lies awake until she does.

Kieran has also kept Josh's hoodie, which was in his car the night before the accident. He has not washed it or worn it. It lies folded on the passenger seat, and when his mother asked whether he wanted to give it back to Josh's parents, he walked out of the kitchen without answering.
moreCases.misread:
Sinéad read Kieran's silence and constant activity as a refusal to grieve, and kept offering the kind of grieving she would have wanted: talking about feelings. Each offer felt to Kieran like pressure, and pushed him further away.

She also took his throwing away the leaflets as a sign that he was in denial, when it was more likely a sign that the leaflets were offering a kind of help that did not fit him.

And by treating counselling as the only proper way to grieve, she sent Kieran a message he heard clearly: that his way was wrong.
moreCases.betterRead:
Doka and Martin describe a continuum from intuitive grieving, mainly through feeling and talking, to instrumental grieving, mainly through thought and activity. Many men, though by no means all, lean towards the instrumental end, and their grief can look from outside like avoidance. The gym, the extra shifts and the silence did not mean Kieran was not grieving. They may have been how he was grieving. Declan's better approach was to offer something to do. He asked Kieran whether he would help him organise a charity football match in Josh's memory, which Josh's parents had mentioned wanting. Kieran agreed at once. Over the next two months, booking pitches, chasing sponsors and recruiting players, he talked about Josh more than he had since the accident: the goals Josh scored, the nicknames, the night they got lost in Dublin. He never once talked about his feelings, and he cried at the match, in front of everyone, when Josh's dad presented the trophy.

Sinéad also stopped leaving leaflets, and started going to watch the training sessions for the match, which gave her and Kieran something to talk about in the car on the way home.

moreCases.title: The colleague who left the meeting
moreCases.scene:
Nadia, forty-four, works in a busy marketing team. Her mother died eight months ago, after a long illness. She took two weeks off, came back and has been, everyone agrees, "amazing": on top of her work, cheerful, efficient. In a Monday meeting, the team is choosing music for a client's advert. Someone plays a clip of an old song. Nadia goes very still, her breath catches, and she gets up and leaves the room without a word.

Her manager, Tom, is irritated. The client presentation is on Wednesday, and walking out of a meeting is not like her. One of her colleagues mutters that it was a bit unprofessional. Another wonders aloud whether she is still "not over it".

Nadia comes back twenty minutes later, red-eyed, apologises and carries on as if nothing has happened.

Nadia has not mentioned her mother at work since she came back. Nobody else has either. Several colleagues have said they did not want to upset her by bringing it up.

Before the meeting, Nadia had been laughing in the kitchen with two colleagues about a television programme. Nothing about her morning suggested that anything was wrong, which is part of why the walk-out surprised everyone so much.
moreCases.misread:
Tom read Nadia's walk-out as unprofessional, and a colleague read it as evidence that she had not recovered as she should. Both treated grief as something that ends, after which any return of it is a problem.

And the colleague's "not over it" carried an assumption that grief should be finished in eight months, which few people who have been bereaved would recognise.

Tom's irritation also came from the deadline, not from Nadia. A manager under pressure is quicker to read any interruption as a problem.
moreCases.betterRead:
Grief comes in waves, often long after a death, and the triggers are frequently small and unpredictable: a smell, a date, a place, a song. The body shows the wave suddenly, as Nadia's did: stillness, a caught breath, an abrupt exit. Eight months is not late for a wave; for many people the first year is full of them, and they continue, less often, for years. Leaving the room was probably the most professional thing Nadia could have done. Tom's better response came after he asked a colleague who knew Nadia well, and learned that the song had been played at her mother's funeral. He went to her desk later, quietly, and said, "I'm sorry about earlier. That must have caught you off guard. Take whatever time you need, and if there's anything that would make work easier for a bit, tell me." She said thank you, and that it was the first time anyone at work had mentioned her mother since she came back.

He also told the rest of the team, with Nadia's permission, that the song had been played at her mother's funeral, so that nobody would wonder about the meeting.

moreCases.title: The girl who played at the wake
moreCases.scene:
Mia, eight, was very close to her grandad, who died suddenly of a stroke. At the funeral she holds her mother's hand and asks a lot of questions: where Grandad is now, whether he can hear them, whether he was frightened. At the wake she plays happily with her cousins under the tables, laughing, eating cake and asking for more lemonade. Her aunt remarks that children are so lucky, they just bounce back.

That night, at bedtime, Mia has a screaming tantrum over a missing sock, kicks her bedroom door and then sobs for an hour, saying she wants Grandad. Over the next few weeks the pattern repeats: happy, ordinary days, and then sudden storms of anger or tears, often at bedtime or over something tiny. She has started wetting the bed again, which she has not done since she was four.

Her father, Sam, does not know whether to be strict about the tantrums or to let them go. He wonders whether something is wrong with her.

Mia has also been asking the same questions again and again: whether Grandad is cold, whether he knows she misses him, whether Mummy is going to die too. Sam has answered them the first few times and is starting to find them hard.

Mia's teacher has also mentioned that she has been quieter in class, and that she drew a picture of her family at the weekend with Grandad in it, standing a little apart, with wings.
moreCases.misread:
The aunt read Mia's play as a sign that she was not affected, and Sam read the later storms as a behaviour problem or a sign that something was wrong. Both readings came from expecting a child's grief to look like an adult's.

Sam's worry that something was wrong also led him towards the strict response, which would have punished Mia for grief she could not yet put into words.

And the aunt's "bounce back" carried a hope that many adults have for children, that they will be spared. The hope is kind, and it can stop adults noticing grief that comes out later.
moreCases.betterRead:
Children often grieve in short bursts, moving quickly between intense grief and ordinary play, which bereavement charities for children sometimes compare to jumping in and out of puddles. Play at a wake is common and healthy, and it does not mean a child has not understood. Grief may then come out sideways, in anger, clinginess, sleep problems, stomach aches or a return to younger behaviours such as bed-wetting, often at bedtime, when the day's distractions end. Sam's better approach combined steadiness with openness. He kept the bedtime routine predictable and calm, treated the bed-wetting without fuss, and made time each evening for Mia to talk about Grandad if she wanted to, using plain words rather than phrases such as "gone to sleep". He told her school what had happened. Over the next few months the storms became fewer, and Mia started a memory box with Grandad's watch and photographs, which she showed to everyone who visited.

Sam also told Mia's teacher about the drawing, and asked the school whether they had any support for bereaved children, which they did.

workedReading.title: The neighbour after the funeral
workedReading.scene:
Shona lives next door to Ray, seventy-eight, whose wife, Iris, died six weeks ago. They have been neighbours for twenty years, friendly over the fence but not close. Iris did most of the talking. At the funeral, Ray seemed composed. Since then, Shona has noticed that his curtains are often closed at midday, that the milk has been left on the step two mornings running, and that his car has not moved for over a week. Iris used to put the bins out; this week nobody did. Shona has not seen Ray at all for four days.

Shona is aware that she barely knows Ray without Iris. She is not sure he will want her help, and she is a little afraid of intruding on a grief she has no part in.

She also knows, from her own mother's death, that the weeks after the funeral were the loneliest of all, when everyone assumed the worst was over and the house went quiet.

steps.label: Notice the change
steps.text:
Shona lists what she has seen: curtains closed in daytime, milk left out, the car unmoved, bins not out, Ray not seen for four days. Each could have an ordinary explanation. Together, against twenty years of a very regular household, they make a pattern of a man who may have withdrawn into the house.

She also notes what she has not seen. Nobody has visited in the past week. His son lives two hundred miles away, and the daughter-in-law who came every day before the funeral has gone home.

She also checks her own reasons. She does not want to be nosy, and she does not want to be the neighbour who noticed nothing. Holding both in mind, she decides that a light, practical knock respects both.

steps.label: Consider the explanations
steps.text:
He might be away, staying with his son. He might be unwell. He might be grieving in the way many people do in the weeks after the funeral, when the visitors stop and the reality arrives, staying in, not eating, not sleeping. He might simply not have known that Iris did the bins. Shona notes that she cannot tell which, and that most of the possibilities call for the same first step.

She also reminds herself that six weeks is often when the visitors have stopped and the casseroles have run out, and when many people feel the loss most sharply.

She also considers that if he were seriously unwell, waiting would be the worst choice. That possibility, small as it is, is one more reason to knock today rather than next week.

steps.label: Knock, with a practical reason
steps.text:
She takes his milk in from the step and knocks, with the bins as her reason: "I've brought your milk in, Ray, and I wondered if you'd like me to put your bins out with mine on Tuesdays for a while." A practical offer is easier to accept than a question about how he is, and it gives both of them something to talk about on the doorstep.

She also chooses mid-morning, when he is most likely to be up, and keeps the milk in her hand, so that she has something to give him and a natural reason to be on his step.

She also prepares herself for him not answering. If he does not, she will try his son's number through a mutual friend, and if she still hears nothing and sees no sign of him, she will call for help.

steps.label: Read what she sees
steps.text:
Ray opens the door in yesterday's clothes. He has not shaved, he looks thinner, and his voice is hoarse, as if he has not used it for days. He thanks her for the milk and says the bins would be a help. He is steady on his feet and his speech is clear, which reassures her that he is not unwell in a way that needs help now. He seems, more than anything, very tired and very alone.

She also notes the house behind him. It smells stale, the post is piled on the mat and there is a single cup on the hall table. Nothing alarming, but a picture of a man who has stopped looking after his home.

She also notices that he has made the effort to come to the door, and to thank her. That small courtesy is a good sign: the man Iris married is still there, under the tiredness.

steps.label: Say her name
steps.text:
Shona says, "I keep thinking about Iris. I miss seeing her in the garden." Ray's face changes. His eyes fill, and then he smiles and says that she would have had something to say about the state of the hedge. He asks Shona whether she would like a cup of tea. She says yes, though she had not planned to stay.

She chooses her words carefully, about Iris rather than about Ray's feelings. Talking about the person who died is often easier than talking about the grief.

Saying Iris's name is also what twenty years of neighbourliness allow. Shona knew her. A stranger saying the same would mean less; a friend's memory of the person is part of what makes it comforting.

steps.label: Offer something specific
steps.text:
Over the tea, Ray talks about Iris for half an hour. When Shona leaves, she does not say "let me know if you need anything". She says, "I'm making a shepherd's pie on Thursday. I'll bring you some round at six." She also asks whether his son knows how he has been, and Ray admits that he has been telling him on the phone that he is fine.

She also gives him a reason to say yes that is not about need. Cooking for one more is no trouble, she says, and she always makes too much.

She also leaves the conversation when Ray starts to tire. Grieving people often have less energy for company than they did, and a short visit that ends well is better than a long one that drains him.

steps.label: Keep going, and know the limits
steps.text:
Shona brings the pie, and keeps doing the bins. She notes in her calendar the date of Iris's birthday and the anniversary of her death. She also keeps an eye on the signs that grief may be more than grief: if Ray stopped eating altogether, could not look after himself, talked about not wanting to go on, or seemed unwell, she would contact his son and his doctor, and if he were in danger, get help at once. Over the following months, Ray's curtains open earlier, his car moves again, and one Sunday he knocks on Shona's door with a cutting from Iris's favourite rose.

She also mentions to Ray, lightly, that his son might like to know how he really is, and offers to have the son's number in case she ever needs it. Ray gives it to her that afternoon.

She also tells Ray, on one of her visits, about a bereavement group that meets at the library on Wednesdays, and says she would walk him there if he ever wanted to try it. He says he will think about it, and in the spring he goes.

moreFailures.title: Judging grief by how it looks
moreFailures.body:
People carry pictures of what grief should look like: tears, a sad face, a quiet withdrawal for a decent length of time, then a gradual return. Real grief rarely matches the picture. It laughs at wakes, goes to the gym, throws itself into work, plays under the tables, and then sobs in a toilet cubicle or storms at bedtime. Judging someone's grief by how it looks, deciding they are not grieving enough, or are grieving too much, or in the wrong way, is one of the most hurtful things people do to the bereaved. Read the person against their own baseline and their own style, not against a picture of grief, and assume that whatever you see is only part of what they are carrying.

It also helps to remember that people often save their hardest grief for when they are alone, or with the one or two people they trust most. What a colleague or an in-law sees is often the composed version, kept up at great cost.

It also helps to remember that grief often shows differently in public and in private. Someone may be steady at work and collapse at home, or the other way round. Neither is the whole truth, and neither is a performance.

Men in particular are often judged for grieving by doing. A father who goes back to work a week after a child's funeral may be told he is cold, when work may be the only place he can stand to be.

moreFailures.title: Avoiding the name
moreFailures.body:
Many people, afraid of upsetting a bereaved person, avoid mentioning the person who died. They talk about the weather, work, anything else. Bereaved people often say that this avoidance is one of the loneliest parts of grief: everyone seems to have forgotten, or to want them to forget. Saying the name rarely causes pain that was not already there, and it usually brings relief. "I was thinking about Iris today." "What was your mum like?" "I remember Josh scoring that goal." If tears come, they are not a sign that you have made things worse. They are often a sign that you have made it safe to grieve.

If you are not sure whether to mention the person, you can ask: "Do you mind if I talk about her?" Most bereaved people say yes, and are grateful to have been asked.

Children notice avoidance too. A child whose parent has died may stop mentioning them if the adults around never do, and conclude that the person, or the grief, is something shameful.

moreFailures.title: Disappearing after the funeral
moreFailures.body:
In the first days after a death, there are visitors, cards, meals and calls. After the funeral, they fall away, often within weeks, just as the full reality of the loss arrives. The hardest months for many bereaved people are the third to the twelfth, and the hardest days are the anniversaries, birthdays and holidays that come round in the first year. A message in month three, a meal in month six, a call on the anniversary, a visit on the first Christmas: these are often remembered for years. Put the dates in your calendar, and use them.

If you were not close enough to visit, a card or message in month three still matters. It tells the person that someone remembered, after the world seemed to forget.

Practical help matters most in these later months: the first time a widow has to deal with the car insurance alone, the first time a widower has to cook Christmas dinner, the first birthday with nobody to buy for.

If you live far away, a regular call, a handwritten letter or a parcel on a hard date can do the same work. What matters is that it keeps coming after everyone else has stopped.

moreFailures.title: Putting grief on a timetable
moreFailures.body:
"Shouldn't he be over it by now?" "It's been a year." "She needs to move on." Grief does not follow a timetable, and pressure to finish it tends to push it underground rather than end it. Most people find that grief changes over time, becoming something they carry alongside their lives rather than something that fills them, but the change is gradual and uneven, and waves continue for years. The question that matters is not how long it has been, but whether the person is able to live their life. If, many months on, grief has stopped someone functioning at all, that is a reason to encourage professional help, not a reason to hurry them.

It also helps to watch your own discomfort. Much of the pressure on bereaved people to move on comes from the people around them, who find grief hard to be near. Noticing that in yourself makes it easier to stay.

It also helps to separate grief from the practical changes that follow a death. Someone who is not yet ready to sort out the wardrobe or sell the car is not stuck in grief; they are choosing their own pace, which is theirs to choose.

questions.a:
The best-known stages, denial, anger, bargaining, depression and acceptance, come from Elisabeth Kübler-Ross's 1969 book on people who were dying, not people who were bereaved, and she later said they were never meant as a fixed sequence. Research on bereavement has not found that most people move through set stages in order. Many people feel several of these things at once, or in no particular order, or not at all, and move back and forth between grief and ordinary life, as the dual process model describes. The idea of stages can be harmful if it makes people feel they are grieving wrongly, or makes others wait for a stage that never comes.

Kübler-Ross's stages are not useless. Some people recognise some of those feelings, and naming them can help. The harm comes only when they are treated as a map that everyone must follow.

If someone you know finds the stages helpful, there is no need to argue with them. Let them use the idea that fits, and offer the dual process model only if they seem to be judging themselves for not feeling the right thing.

questions.q: Is it normal not to cry?
questions.a:
Yes. Many people grieve deeply without crying much, or cry only in private, or cry weeks later at something unexpected. George Bonanno's research on bereavement found that many people show a pattern he called resilience: real sorrow, but little lasting disruption to their daily lives, and this was not a sign that they had loved the person less. Instrumental grievers, in Doka and Martin's terms, may grieve mainly through activity. Not crying is not a problem in itself. What matters more is whether the person has some way of carrying the loss, and some people around them who will let them carry it in their own way.

It also helps to know that crying can come at strange times: at a film, at a stranger's kindness, years later. Grief that did not show at the funeral may show at a wedding, a birth or a song in a shop.

It can also help to tell someone who has not cried that it is all right not to. Some people worry that their dry eyes mean something is wrong with them, and are relieved to hear that grief takes many forms.

Less than you fear you need to. "I'm so sorry" is enough to start. Saying the person's name, "I'm so sorry about Frank", is better. "Tell me about him" invites the stories many bereaved people want to tell. Avoid phrases that shrink or explain the loss: at least he had a long life, she's in a better place, everything happens for a reason, I know how you feel. If you do not know what to say, it is fine to say so: "I don't know what to say, but I wanted you to know I'm thinking of you." Then listen, and let silences happen. Your presence says more than your words.

It also helps to follow their lead. If they want to talk about the funeral, the illness or the last conversation, listen. If they want to talk about football, talk about football. Both are grief.

It also helps to know that you do not need to make them feel better. Grief is not a problem you can solve, and trying to solve it usually leads to the phrases that hurt. Your job is to be there while they feel it.

questions.q: Should I mention the person who died months later?
questions.a:
Usually, yes. Many bereaved people say that one of the hardest things about the months after a death is that everyone else seems to have moved on and stopped mentioning the person, as if they had never existed. A mention months or years later, on an anniversary, at a birthday, or simply because something reminded you, often brings comfort. "I was thinking about your dad today. He'd have loved this." If the person does not want to talk, they will say so, and you will have lost nothing. Take your cue from them, and do not assume that silence is what they want.

Families often say that the people they remember most are not the ones who said the right thing at the funeral, but the ones who were still mentioning the person a year later.

Writing a few lines in a card on an anniversary, with a memory of the person, can mean a great deal. People often keep such cards for years, long after the flowers are gone.

There is no timetable. For most people, the most intense grief eases over the first year or two, and then becomes something they carry, returning in waves on anniversaries and at unexpected moments for the rest of their lives. That is ordinary. For a minority, grief stays as intense and disabling as at the start for many months, and psychiatry now recognises this as prolonged grief disorder: the World Health Organization's classification looks for it at least six months after a death, and the American system at least twelve months after. If someone you know seems stuck in this way, encourage them, gently, to talk to their doctor about bereavement support.

It also helps to know that grief can change shape over time. Some people find the second year harder than the first, because the numbness has worn off and the support has gone.

It also helps to know that bereavement support is available in many places, from charities, hospices, faith groups and GP surgeries, and that people can use it at any point, not only in the first weeks.

If you are the one grieving, it may help to know that there is no deadline for asking for support. Many people seek help only in the second or third year, when they realise the grief has not eased as they expected.

questions.q: Can grief make people physically ill?
questions.a:
It can affect the body in many ways. Mostofsky and colleagues found that the risk of a heart attack was sharply raised in the day after the death of someone significant, and fell over the following weeks. Grief also disrupts sleep and appetite, lowers energy, and can make people forget to look after themselves: to eat, to take their medicines, to go to appointments. Bereaved people, especially older people and those with heart conditions, may benefit from a check-up in the weeks after a death. A practical friend can help by asking about medicines and meals, as Andy did with his father, rather than only about feelings.

Grief can also affect concentration and memory. Bereaved people often find that they forget appointments, lose things and cannot focus at work, and it helps them to know that this is common and usually eases.

It may also help to make the practical things easier: offering to drive them to the doctor, putting medicines into a weekly pill box, or making sure there is food in the fridge that needs no cooking.

watch.title: We don't move on from grief. We move forward with it
watch.notice: Nora McInerny on living alongside grief rather than getting over it. Notice what she says about how grieving people are expected to look and behave, and how far that is from reality.

reviewPrompt: This week, put the anniversary of one friend's loss in your calendar, and send them a message on the day that mentions the person by name.
